title: The phone in the kitchen
text:
Maya's screen time report said six hours and forty minutes a day. She checked it twice, because it felt impossible.

She didn't delete anything. She moved her phone charger from the bedroom to the kitchen.

The first three nights were strange. She reached for a phone that wasn't there, twice each night. On the fourth night she read eleven pages of a book she had started in April.

Two weeks later her screen time was four hours. Still high, but the last hour of every day had changed completely. She fell asleep faster and stopped doomscrolling the news at midnight.

Her colleague tried the same thing and failed, because he used his phone as an alarm clock. So he bought a seven-euro alarm clock, and then it worked.

Maya makes no big claims about it. She didn't become a different person or take up meditation. She says only that she gets an extra forty minutes at the end of the day, and she chooses what happens in them.

The charger is still in the kitchen. That's the whole system.

options: She moved her phone charger to the kitchen

questions.q: What happened in the first few nights?
options: She reached for a phone that wasn't there

questions.q: Why did her colleague fail at first?
options: He used his phone as an alarm clock

questions.q: What does Maya claim about the change?
options: She gained forty minutes she now chooses how to use
She became a completely different person
She stopped using her phone entirely

title: Saying no in November
text:
By November, Krasimir was saying yes to everything. Two committees, a weekend course, a neighbour's renovation, and a job that already filled the week.

He wasn't enjoying any of it. He was attending all of it.

The change started with an uncomfortable exercise his sister suggested. He wrote down every commitment and beside each one wrote why he had agreed. Seven of the eleven answers were some version of "it felt rude to refuse".

He cancelled three things in one evening. All three replies were friendly. Nobody was offended, which annoyed him slightly, because it meant the fear had been entirely his own.

Setting boundaries felt rude for about two weeks. Then it felt normal.

What surprised him most was not the free time. It was that the things he kept got better. He read for the course instead of skimming. He actually talked to people at the one committee he stayed on.

His rule now is simple and slightly annoying to everyone who asks him for something: he says he'll answer tomorrow. Most of the pressure to say yes lives in the first thirty seconds.

questions.q: Why had Krasimir agreed to most of his commitments?
What happened when he cancelled three things?
options: Everyone replied in a friendly way
Two people stopped speaking to him
The things he kept became better
He answers requests the following day
He only says yes in writing
